lesson_1.title: Best Case Scenario
task: Big-O notation, and our Complexity Analyzer, evaluate the **Worst Case** scenario. If you write a loop, the analyzer assumes it will run entirely, grading it as O(n).

But what if Cody gets lucky and finds his target on the very first try? That's the **Best Case** (Omega Ω)! To avoid the analyzer's worst-case grading, let's simulate this by writing a direct check without a loop.

optimizations.title: Optimize Duplicate Search
task: Welcome to the Optimization Challenge! We have pre-loaded a `find_duplicates` function that uses a nested loop to check every number against every other number. If you check the Complexity tab, you'll see this causes a terribly slow O(n²) time complexity.
Refactor the loaded function to run in lightning-fast O(n) Linear Time.
1. Locate and **delete the inner loop block** from the workspace.
2. Above the remaining single loop, create a new variable (e.g., `seen`) and set it to an empty list or dictionary.
3. Inside the loop, add an `if` block: check if the current item is already in your `seen` collection.
4. If it is, return that item immediately!
5. If it is not, add the current item to your `seen` collection so you can remember it for the next iterations.
6. Keep the final `return -1` at the very bottom. Run the tests to claim your O(n) Gold Medal!

optimizations.title: Optimize Two Sum
task: The classic Two Sum problem! We've pre-loaded a brute-force algorithm that uses an O(n²) nested loop to check every possible pair of numbers to see if they add up to the target.
Refactor the loaded algorithm to find the pair in a single O(n) pass by utilizing O(n) Space.
1. Locate and **delete the inner loop block** to break the O(n²) bottleneck.
2. Before your loop, create a dictionary/list variable (e.g., `history`) to act as a Hash Map.
3. Inside the single loop, create a variable `difference` and use a Math block to set it to `target - current item`.
4. Add an `if` block: If the `difference` already exists in your `history`, you found the pair! Return them as a list.
5. If not, add the current item to your `history` and let the loop continue.
6. Run the code and watch your execution time drop to O(n)!
